title: KV Cache-Aware Routing and P/D Disaggregation on Kubernetes — Yuchen Fama & Ashish Kamra, Red Hat

summary:
Yuchen and Ashish frame llm-d as a CNCF-hosted, Kubernetes-native distributed inference framework addressing the volatility of agentic workloads—multi-turn sessions up to 3,000 turns, cache hit rates above 90%, and input-to-output token ratios exceeding 100:1. Because clients control prompt structure, KV caches become volatile, motivating cache-aware routing via the endpoint picker (EP) plugin that scores pods on load and KV/prefix availability, plus offload tiers (NVMe/SSD, XF, Mooncake) and eviction policies like session pinning. A live demo showed ~3s for a cold first turn, ~1s for a same-pod cache hit, and ~3s again when a fresh system prompt routed to a different pod. With a ~10x Anthropic pricing gap between cached and uncached tokens, routing is a higher-leverage optimization than adding GPUs.

Ashish motivates PD disaggregation through phase interference: prefill is compute-bound/bursty, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound/latency-sensitive, and aggregated pods let long prefill bursts stall streaming decode. llm-d's PD flow uses EP-driven routing to optimal prefill/decode workers, the prefill worker emits KV transfer metadata, and the decode worker pulls KV across the network fabric. Internal results on gpt-oss 120B across 16 H100s cut P99 ITL from ~900ms (aggregated) to ~100ms (PD), with the biggest gains in the middle concurrency band and roughly tied at both ends. A second benchmark (64 H100s, three prefill/five decode, 5,000 ISL/500 OSL) showed PD dominating across the entire interactivity spectrum.

Ashish's decision matrix: PD helps with long context, large models enabling rich parallelism, middle concurrency, strict ITL streaming, and requires RDMA/RoCE. Stay aggregated for short/moderate context, low concurrency, strict TTFT tuning, or without high-speed fabrics. Architectural takeaways include dynamic PD ratio matching, independent autoscaling of prefill/decode pools, and combining tensor/data/expert parallelism. The closing GLM 5.2 case study on H200s used three prefill workers and one decode worker with TP1/DP8/EP8, NIXL-based KV transfer, and a leader worker set group, achieving 4x faster TTFT and 60% more requests on a 45:1 ISL:OSL agentic dataset.

sections.title: What public inference benchmarks leave out (0:00)
sections.summary: Ashish opens by noting public inference benchmarks report steady-state, sanitized numbers and miss the chaos of multi-turn agentic interactions with massive context fluctuations. He introduces the session focus on KV cache-aware routing and PD disaggregation.

sections.title: Red Hat's inference stack and the agenda (1:28)
sections.summary: Yuchen and Ashish introduce themselves. Yuchen previews analysis of agentic-era inference behavior; Ashish previews PD mechanics and results; Yuchen closes with a GLM case study. They cite free deeplearning.ai course and Red Hat developer portal blogs, and note Red Hat's role in vLLM, llm-d, llm-compressor, llm-spec-dec, and guideLLM.

sections.title: Agentic traces: 3,000 turns, 90% cache hits, 100:1 ratios (3:29)
sections.summary: Yuchen argues we are moving from classic to agentic inference. Real-world workloads like SWE-bench and cloud coding show multi-turn counts from a few to 3,000, cache hit rates exceeding 90%, input:output token ratios over 100:1, and complex context distributions (e.g., sub-agent fan-out). Red Hat collaborated with Google and IBM on a trace replay tool added to inference-perf.

sections.title: Volatile cache and the 10x cached token gap (5:12)
sections.summary: Optimization shifts from steady-state throughput to interactive latency and client-driven context. KV cache management becomes volatile, requiring prefix routing tied into scheduling, and metrics must separate cached throughput. Anthropic API pricing shows ~10x cost between cached and uncached tokens, making cache-aware routing high-leverage.

sections.title: How llm-d routes: endpoint picker, offload tiers, eviction (6:28)
sections.summary: llm-d's router uses flexible Endpoint Picker (EP) plugins that score pods on load (running/waiting requests) and KV cache/prefix availability to route to the optimal pod. Cache management supports hot/warm/cold tiers with offloads to NVMe/SSD and XF file system, plus KV-centric stores like Mooncake, and eviction policies including priority and session pinning.

sections.title: Demo: cache hits, pod affinity, 3s vs 1s (7:46)
sections.summary: Live demo: first request populates cache with no hit, ~3s; second turn reuses system prompt on the same pod, ~1s; third turn with a different system prompt routes to a different pod and again ~3s; fourth turn with same system prompt reuses cache at ~1s. Yuchen notes this helps TTFT but for agentic workloads inter-token latency matters too, motivating PD disaggregation.

sections.title: What llm-d is and why prefill and decode interfere (9:28)
sections.summary: Ashish defines llm-d as a CNCF-hosted, Kubernetes-native (and non-K8s) distributed inference framework with workload APIs (LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet) and autoscalers. He explains phase interference: prefill is compute-bound/bursty, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound/latency-sensitive, and an aggregated pod can let a long prefill stall ongoing decode token generation.

sections.title: How disaggregation works in practice (12:03)
sections.summary: In llm-d's PD flow, the gateway router uses EP to select optimal prefill and decode workers. The prefill worker processes the prompt, builds the KV cache, and outputs KV transfer metadata; the target decode worker pulls the KV cache across the network fabric using that metadata.

sections.title: P99 inter-token latency: 900ms vs 100ms (13:08)
sections.summary: Internal Red Hat graph for gpt-oss 120B across 16 H100s shows aggregated P99 ITL hovering around 900ms with fluctuations, while PD drops P99 ITL to about 100ms with a much smoother curve.

sections.title: Where PD shines across the concurrency curve (14:14)
sections.summary: Ashish presents benchmark charts showing PD advantages across concurrency regimes. A highly multi-turn workload (10,000 token prefix, 128 tokens per turn) on gpt-oss 120B with 4-replica aggregated TP4 vs 2 prefill/2 decode TP4 shows PD roughly tied with aggregated at low and high concurrency, with the biggest wins in the middle. Another chart with 64 H100s (8 replicas TP8 aggregated vs 3 prefill/5 decode TP8, 5,000 ISL/500 OSL) shows PD dominating across the entire interactivity spectrum. KV-cache-aware routing alone yields measurable gains over standard aggregated Kubernetes scheduling.

sections.title: When to use PD, and when to stay aggregated (15:45)
sections.summary: Ashish walks through a decision matrix. PD helps when managing long context with high ISL/OSL ratios, serving large models amenable to rich parallelism, operating in the middle concurrency regime, or needing strict ITL streaming. PD requires an RDMA or RoCE fabric for KV cache transfer. Stay aggregated for short/moderate context, any model size at low concurrency, when you need strict TTFT tuning, or when you lack the network fabric to transfer KV caches.

sections.title: Architectural takeaways for llm-d design (17:30)
sections.summary: Ashish summarizes the multi-dimensional design space: schedulers must constantly evaluate SLO targets, QEPs, KV cache locality, PD ratios, and network topology to route to the optimal pod. PD design needs dynamic PD ratio matching that adapts with autoscaling, independent autoscaling of PD pools, and continuous tuning of tensor and data parallelism to meet SLOs.

sections.title: GLM 5.2 on H200s: 4x faster TTFT (18:10)
sections.summary: Yuchen closes with a GLM 5.2 case study on H200s (since customers lack B200s). The architecture uses three prefill workers optimized for high throughput and one dedicated decode worker optimized for low latency, with NIXL for KV transfer, LeaderWorkerSet groups with TP1/DP8/EP8, and modular scaling. On a 45:1 ISL/OSL agentic dataset with 2 prefill/1 decode, they achieved 4x faster TTFT and 60% more requests. Future work includes lower TTFT and more prefill replicas. The talk closes with an invitation to join the upstream llm-d SIG and visit the booth, noting open collaboration with CoreWeave, Google, IBM, Nvidia, and other ecosystem partners.
